claims.text: The initial material is a partially sintered W skeleton or connected W regions.
The proposed intervention is molten-Cu infiltration of the W preform using hot isostatic pressing.
HIP infiltration is to be conducted at at least 100 MPa.
HIP infiltration is to be conducted at 1100–1200 °C in an inert environment.
HIP infiltration will produce near-complete Cu infiltration and densification of the W skeleton.
High hydrostatic pressure forces molten Cu into residual pores in the W skeleton.
The applied pressure promotes strong W–Cu interfacial bonding.
Pore filling and stronger interfacial bonding mitigate phase separation and void formation.
HIP infiltration will yield lower porosity and fewer interfacial defects than conventional infiltration or spark-plasma sintering.
HIP infiltration will yield a more homogeneous W–Cu composite than conventional infiltration or spark-plasma sintering.
HIP infiltration will provide superior mechanical strength and durability relative to conventional infiltration or spark-plasma sintering.
HIP infiltration will provide higher thermal conductivity under operational stress than conventional infiltration or spark-plasma sintering.
Standard infiltration and spark-plasma sintering often leave residual pores or inhomogeneous W–Cu distributions.
The proposed process has currently been demonstrated only at laboratory scale.
Large-scale industrial feasibility and in-reactor performance remain unvalidated.
Residual stresses and possible interfacial reactions at high infiltration pressure may reduce microstructural consistency.
Failure of the HIP material to improve porosity, mechanical properties, or thermal conductivity relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
